e: Standard-IA (multi-AZ, so images aren't lost) fits the infrequently accessed period from day 180, Glacier Instant Retrieval after 360 days archives the images yet keeps millisecond access, and Deep Archive after 5 years meets the 12-hour retrieval for auditors at the lowest cost. One Zone-IA risks data loss, and Flexible Retrieval isn't instant.

A transient cluster runs only for the 6-hour job (cheaper than long-running), the primary and core nodes (which hold HDFS data) stay on On-Demand so no data is lost, and the task nodes (no data) run on cheap Spot Instances. Core nodes on Spot risk data loss.

An EventBridge rule reacting to CloudTrail resource-creation events invokes a Lambda function that looks up the creating user's cost center in the RDS database and tags the new resource automatically. SCPs and tag-on-schedule or default tag approaches don't tag with the per-user value.

CloudFront with an S3 bucket serves static content, an ALB with ECS on Fargate runs the PHP application as a managed, highly available service, and ElastiCache for Redis across multiple AZs replaces the local Redis for sessions. The other options keep a single EC2 instance or don't fit PHP on Lambda.

An Application Load Balancer supports session affinity (sticky sessions) and AWS WAF, so create a public ALB for the target group and associate a WAF web ACL with it. NLBs don't support sticky sessions the same way or WAF, and Gateway Load Balancers aren't public endpoints.

Images requested only once or twice a year are best in S3 Standard-IA (lower storage cost, highly available), and S3 can serve them directly through a static website without EC2. EBS or EFS with EC2 cost more and are less available.

A customer managed prefix list holding the office CIDRs, shared across the organization with AWS RAM, can be referenced in the security groups of every account, so updating the list updates all the rules in one place at no extra cost. Firewall Manager and Security Hub options cost more or aren't designed for this.

FSx for NetApp ONTAP supports both NFS and SMB multi-protocol access with low latency, and compute optimized instances in a cluster placement group give the lowest network latency between instances. Lustre doesn't support SMB, OpenZFS doesn't provide the same multi-protocol, and partition placement groups aren't for low latency.

The VPN is 90% utilized, so there's little bandwidth left to move 50 TB in 2 weeks, and Direct Connect takes too long to provision. A Snowball Edge Storage Optimized device transfers securely offline within the window.

Peak hours occur at the same time every day and performance is slow only at the start, while reactive scaling lags behind demand. Scheduled scaling launches instances before the peak begins so capacity is ready on time.

RDS Proxy pools and shares database connections so applications that scale up on weekends and peaks don't overwhelm the database, and it requires only switching the endpoint, with little operational overhead. DynamoDB, a custom EC2 proxy, or a Lambda proxy are wrong or need more effort.

Snapshot costs grow because old snapshots accumulate, so delete the nonessential ones and use Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager to create and expire snapshots automatically per policy, which minimizes ongoing effort. Shrinking volumes manually or deleting snapshots once doesn't stop the growth.

A bucket policy limiting access to the ECS task execution role restricts the S3 data to the ECS cluster, and a security group on the RDS database that allows connections only from the subnets of the ECS tasks restricts database access to the cluster. KMS keys alone don't restrict network or principal access, and an S3 endpoint policy alone lets any resource in the VPC reach the bucket.

Burstable instances in unlimited mode can sustain CPU at far above baseline during the short, sudden 10x spikes that occur twice a month, and scaling on request count adds instances automatically as demand rises. Scheduled scaling can't predict these spikes, and compute optimized instances cost more all the time.

CloudFormation sets up the infrastructure as code with automation and repeatability, and AWS Config records and audits every incremental configuration change to resources. Organizations doesn't build infrastructure, and Service Catalog doesn't track configuration changes.

An RDS for MySQL Multi-AZ instance makes the database highly available with no application change (still MySQL), and an ALB with an Auto Scaling group across two AZs makes the stateless Python tier highly available. Internet gateways are VPC-level (already redundant), DynamoDB would require code changes, and DataSync doesn't replicate databases.

Gateway endpoints for S3 can't be reached from on premises, but interface endpoints (PrivateLink) for S3 can be accessed from both the VPC and the on-premises network over Direct Connect, keeping traffic off the internet. Transit Gateway and KMS don't provide private S3 access.

An Organizations tag policy defines the allowed values for the application name tag and can enforce compliance across the organization's accounts (with enforcement for supported resources). IAM groups, cross-account roles, and Resource Groups don't validate tag values on creation.

Secrets Manager integrates with RDS for PostgreSQL and can manage the master user password and rotate it automatically on a schedule such as 30 days, with the least overhead. Custom Lambda rotation or manual CLI changes need more work, and Parameter Store has no native rotation.

The company knows the exact read and write rates, and the tests are short, so provisioned mode with the capacity set to the known rates (and reduced when the test isn't running) is cheaper than on-demand's per-request pricing. Reserved capacity isn't worth it for a 4-hour weekly workload.

AWS Cost Anomaly Detection uses machine learning to detect unusual spend and notifies the responsible stakeholders through alerts, which is exactly the need. Zero-spend budgets, Pricing Calculator, and CloudWatch don't detect anomalies in cost.

A Glue crawler infers the schema of the clickstream data in S3 and populates the Data Catalog, and Athena queries it with SQL immediately, serverless with minimal overhead. Spark on EMR or Glue jobs and Kinesis Data Analytics need more setup or aren't for S3 data.

An S3 File Gateway keeps the SMB access and extends storage into S3, and a lifecycle policy moves files to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 7 days, whose standard retrieval takes within about 12 hours, meeting the 24-hour maximum at the lowest cost. FSx File Gateway is for FSx, and per-user S3 access changes how users work.

A read replica takes read traffic off the primary database, and an ElastiCache cache for query results reduces the number of reads hitting the database. RDS instances don't auto scale compute, and a Multi-AZ standby can't serve reads.

EBS snapshot lock prevents snapshots from being deleted (by anyone, for a set duration) without changing the storage administrator's IAM rights, with little effort. A deny policy changes administrator rights, and Recycle Bin only lets you recover snapshots after deletion.
